[PDF page 1]
A REPORT ON TAX CREDITS
IN THE STATE OF MISSOURI

January 2025

Isabel Warner, PhD
MOST Policy Initiative

[PDF page 2]
Executive Summary

Tax credits, also known as tax expenditures, reduce the tax burden of individuals and
entities and result in a reduction of state income. Tax credits are intended to stimulate or
encourage specific sectors, entities, or behavior. Unlike spending programs, tax credits
have less oversight, legislative control, or accountability, and often do not require the same
periodic legislative reauthorization or even review.

Missouri currently administers 69 tax credit programs across multiple departments. Of
these, 58 are still authorized and have not been sunset. The remaining 11 have outstanding
redemptions which taxpayers will claim in the coming years. Departments have control
over tax credit issuances but are typically constrained by authorization and issuance
amounts set by statute.

In 2024, Missouri authorized $518.5 million in tax credits, issued $429.6 million of those,
and saw more than $906.9 million redeemed. The SALT Parity Act to reduce double taxation
for businesses has the highest dollar amount of redemptions, at more than $396 million.
This is trailed by the next highest redemption amount for the Missouri Works Credit, which
is the combination of four credit programs, at $114 million. The Low-Income Housing Tax
Credit follows with nearly $99 million in redemptions. On the opposite end of the
spectrum, 21 credits had no redemptions in 2024. Of these, 12 are still active and have not
been sunset.

States typically focus on sunset measures as a way to manage tax credits and force
periodic reviews. Research suggests that tax credits are most effective when they are
tailored to meet a specific need over a defined time frame. However, it also suggests that
sunsets benefit entities with resources to continually lobby for reauthorization.

Over time, Missouri’s tax credits have increased slightly as a portion of the budget. In 1998
tax credits were equivalent to approximately 1.7% of state revenue, while by 2012 they
amounted to more than 7%, and in 2024 make up roughly 6%.

Tax credits and their impacts are difficult to compare. The only thing all tax credits have in
common is they reduce tax liability. Several frameworks have been developed to assess the
direct and indirect impacts of tax credits, and these are discussed in this report.

Finally, while departments administer credits, the Missouri legislature is ultimately
responsible to its constituents for the oversight and management of tax credits.

Introduction

Primer on Tax Credits

What are tax credits and how do they work?
Tax credits reduce the tax liability that individuals and businesses may owe (GAO 2024, IRS
2023a, IRS 2023b). They are claimed on a tax return form and can result in a lower tax bill
and even an increased refund amount. They have the same net effect on state revenue as a
spending program (GAO 2024, Curchin v. Missouri Industrial Development Board 1987).

Individual Tax Credits
Individual tax credits can be refundable or non-refundable. If a refundable tax credit
amount is higher than what an individual owes, they can receive the difference back in  their
refund (IRS 2023b). By contrast, non-refundable credits do not return any left-over amount
once the individual’s tax liability is zero (Figure 1).

Individual tax credits at the federal level include the earned income tax credit, the
American opportunity tax credit, family and dependent credits, income and savings credits,
homeowner credits, electric vehicle credits, and health care credits (IRS 2023b).

In Missouri, tax credits may apply to both businesses and individuals that pay income
taxes. For example, the now defunct Champion for Children tax credit was available to any
entity liable for income tax that makes a contribution to a qualified agency (MO
Department of Revenue 2024a).

Figure 1. Example of refundable and non-refundable tax credit on final tax bill.
In this example, both situations have the same amount of tax owed, and the same size of
tax credit. However, in a refundable tax credit scenario, the difference between the tax
owed and tax credit amount is returned as a refund to the individual. In a non-refundable
scenario, the individuals tax burden is zero. The final tax bill equals the tax owed minus the
tax credit amount. If the tax credit is larger than the individuals’ tax bill, and the tax credit is
refundable, that amount will be returned to the taxpayer (left). If the tax credit is not
refundable, the taxpayer will owe no taxes (right).

Business Tax Credits
Unlike individual income tax credits, business tax credits can be carried forward from prior
years (IRS 2023a). Credits may also be carried back from later years, to reduce past tax
burdens. The credit is subtracted directly from the taxes a business owes.

At the federal level, businesses are eligible for more than 30 tax credits (IRS 2023a). These
include but are not limited to:

•  employee retention credits
•  investment credits

8

[PDF page 10]
•  work opportunity credits
•  credits for employer-provided childcare facilities and services
•  credits for small employers starting pension plans
•  credits for small employers providing health insurance
•  employer credits for paid family and medical leave

Sellable, Assignable, and Transferrable Credits
Some tax credits can be sold, assigned, or transferred to other entities. Entities that pay
income tax can transfer pieces or the entirety of their tax credit to a third-party buyer in
exchange for cash (IRS 2024a). The terms and price are determined by the buyer and seller.

Credits can only be sold once, and sellers can decide to sell a set dollar amount or
percentage of their credits (Norton Rose Fulbright 2023). The cash received from a tax
credit sale is not included in the seller’s taxable income (Office of Energy Efficiency &
Renewable Energy 2024). Similarly, the cash used to pay for a tax credit is not deductible
from the buyer’s taxable income.

All or a portion of the following credits can be transferred (IRS 2024a):

•  Energy credit (Section 48)
•  Clean electricity investment credit (48E)
•  Renewable electricity production credit (45)
•  Clean electricity production credit (45Y)
•  Zero-emission nuclear power production credit (45U)
•  Advanced manufacturing production credit (45X)
•  Clean hydrogen production credit (45V)
•  Clean fuel production credit (45Z)
•  Carbon oxide sequestration credit (45Q)
•  Credit for alternative fuel vehicle refueling/recharging property (30C)
•  Qualified advanced energy project credit (48C)

Elective Pay
Entities that do not qualify to sell, assign, or transfer credits are eligible for elective pay.
Elective pay allows entities that would otherwise not qualify for tax credits, because they
do not owe federal income tax, to benefit from clean energy tax credits (IRS 2024b). The
credit amount is treated as a payment, which is then counted as overpayment (due to tax
exempt status) and refunded to the entity (IRS 2024a).

Eligible entities include tax-exempt organizations, states, and political subdivisions (IRS
2024a). Tax exempt organizations include but are not limited to:

[PDF page 11]
•  public charities
•  private foundations
•  social welfare organizations
•  labor organizations
•  business leagues
•  some homeowners’ associations

States include the District of Columbia, U.S. territories, and all agencies and
instrumentalities of the state or territory. Political subdivisions include and are not limited
to:

•  cities
•  counties
•  water districts
•  school districts
•  economic development agencies
•  public universities
•  public hospitals

They also include Indian tribal governments, Alaska Native Corporations, the Tennessee
Valley Authority, and rural electric cooperatives.

There are special rules for clean energy tax credits, and taxpayers that do not typically
qualify may apply. There are additional rules if the taxpayer is a partnership or an S
corporation, but generally taxpayers may apply if they own property that qualifi  es for the
section 45Q credit for carbon oxide sequestration, the section 45V credit for production of
clean hydrogen, or the section 45X credit for advanced manufacturing production (  IRS
2024a).

Outside of these exceptions, elective pay is used for the same credits as listed in  Sellable,
Assignable, and Transferrable Credits, and includes the commercial clean vehicle credit
(Section 45W) (IRS 2024a).

In addition, higher credit amounts are offered to projects that pay prevailing wages and
used registered apprentices, are located in low-income communities or energy
communities, or meet certain domestic content requirements (U.S. Department of Labor
2024). Projects can meet domestic content requirements by using the required amount of
domestically produced steel, iron, or manufactured products (IRS 2024a). Energy
communities or historical energy communities are areas where energy production was a
major industry, including areas with closed coal mines or coal-fired power plants (U.S.

2024). It can also apply to projects in areas with brownfield sites (contaminated
properties), areas with significant employment or tax revenue from fossil fuels, especially
those with high unemployment (EPA 2024, IRS 2024a).
How does Missouri administer tax credits?
Missouri tax credits are passed in statute, where their parameters and governance are
outlined. These include but are not limited  to whether the credits are refundable or non  -
refundable, any caps on the dollar amounts of credits, sunset provisions, rulemaking
authority, the type of taxes eligible (income, bank, corporate, etc.), carry forward or
backward limits, whether the credit is sellable or transferable, and the sub-types of credits.
Finally, statutes determine which entities or officials have the capacity to authorize and
issue tax credits (Gross et al. 2012).

Legal Framework for Missouri Tax Credits
According to Missouri’s Supreme Court in Curchin v. Missouri Industrial Development
Board 1987:

“a tax credit is as much a grant of public money or property and is as much a
drain on the State’s coffers as would be an outright payment by the State.”

In some literature, tax credits are referred to as tax expenditures, because they have the
same net effect on government budgets as spending programs (GAO 2024). Tax
expenditures technically refer not only to tax credits, but also tax deductions, exclusions,
exemptions, deferrals, and preferential tax rates. Tax expenditures are not subject to the
appropriations process and are typically not subject to reauthorization or repeated
legislative approval. Because of this, they operate like mandatory spending programs (e.g.
Medicare).

However, unlike most spending programs, Missouri citizens cannot challenge a tax credit or
its awarding without a “direct and particular connection to it” even if they feel it is a misuse
of public funds (Maanzara, et al. v. State of Missouri, et al. 2011, Van Matre et al. 2012).
Relatedly, tax credits cannot be funded by default by the issuance of revenue bonds, as
these bonds effectively constitute state-funded grants to favored private entities, which are
unconstitutional (Missouri Constitution Article III §39(a), Missouri Constitution Article III
§39). Ultimately, it is the duty of the Legislative and Executive branches to ensure that tax
credits are constitutional, since they are virtually unchallengeable in court (Van Matre et al.
2012).

Authorization, Issuance, and Redemption  – Tax Credit Process
Authorization amount is the highest dollar amount that a tax credit can be issued for.  This is
typically the amount that is budgeted for the tax credit, and is set either by the legislature in
statute, or delegated to the agency director. Directors typically include authorization
amounts in their annual budget requests to the legislature (  MO Legislative Library, personal
communication).

The issued amount is the amount of credits that are  confirmed by the department as the
managing entity, while the redeemed credits are those that have been  claimed (Gross et al.
2012). Because business credits can be carried forward or back, the authorization  limit for
a particular year may not match the issued or redeemed amounts  .

For example, the Affordable Housing Assistance Tax Credit Program has an annual cap of
$11 million, with $10 million for production credits, i.e. costs associated with the
production of affordable housing, and $1 million for operating credits, i.e. costs associated
with managing or operating affordable housing (RSMo 32.105, 32.110, 32.111, 32.112,
32.115, 32.117, 32.120, 32.125). In any given year, the department administering the credit
may issue as much as those authorization limits, however the redemptions may come from
issuances in previous years, despite authorization limits remaining the same (Gross et al.
2012).

Entitled vs. Discretionary Tax Credits
Tax credits in Missouri fall into two categories: entitled and discretionary.  For entitled
credits, an entity is automatically eligible (entitled) to receive the credit. Entitled credits are
then applied when an individual or entity files a tax return  . These include things like
property tax credits for surviving spouses of peace officers, credits for donations to things
like diaper banks or domestic violence shelters, or credits for headquartering a large
business (with a minimum of $20 million invested annually) in Missouri (RSMo 135.090,
135.550, 135.621, 135.100-135.258, Figure 2).

Discretionary credits require issuance by managing departments (Gross et al. 2012). For a
discretionary credit, a department will have an amount it is authorized to issue, and entities
will apply up until that limit is reached. However, in many cases, entities have multiple
years to claim the credit on their tax returns, determined by the statute. This carry forward
or carry back amount allows entities to claim credits on previous or future tax returns, in
years the credit was not issued (Office of Administration 2024, Figure 3). The carry forward
or back amount also applies to issued credits that are sold. As long as the credit is issued
to the entity, and within the carry forward or back limit, the taxpayer is able to redeem it.
Because of this, departments may see higher or lower redemptions than were issued in a

given year. These issued but non-redeemed credits are “outstanding,” and may last beyond
the sunset of the credit (Figure 4).

Similarly, credits may have higher authorization limits than the amount issued. If not
enough entities apply, or are turned away, department issuances may be lower than the
amount they are authorized to credit. In this way, some credits remain in statute but have
no “outstanding” redemptions – either not enough entities have applied for issuance, or all
entities that were issued have redeemed the credits’ value (Figure 5).

Limits for discretionary credits are often set in the statute that establishes the credit and
can remain static if not updated (Office of Administration 2024, Gross et al. 2012). Some
discretionary limits are indexed to other values or are set by departments.

Each tax credit is unique because it is defined by statute, and while the above rules are
general operating procedures for tax credit issuance and redemptions, there are many
deviations. For example, some may give departments the ability to issue credits above
authorization limits, some create tax credits that are both discretionary and entitled, and
some may have no carry forward or back provisions at all (RSMo 135.100-135.258,
620.2000-620.2020, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5).

Overview of the number and dollar amount of tax credits in MO.
In Fiscal Year (FY) 2025, the state of Missouri will have 69 tax credits, 58 of which will not be
sunset (Office of Administration 2024). In FY24 $906.9 million was redeemed in tax credits
(Office of Administration, personal communication). By contrast, in 2010, MO had 61 tax
credits, with $521.5 million in redemptions, while in 1998 MO had $102.7 million in
redemptions (Gross et al. 2010, Figure 6).

In 2012, tax credits cost the state approximately more than $629 million (Gross et al. 2012).
This was more than 7% of the state’s $8.64 billion budget. At that time, the ten programs
with the most redemptions constituted 87% of all redemptions (Figure 8). Similarly, the ten
programs with the largest authorization amounts constituted 93% of all authorizations
(Figure 7). For instance, the Low-Income Housing tax credit (LIHTC) accounted for nearly
$180 million in authorizations and $164 million in redemptions in FY 2012 (Figure 7, Figure
8). In comparison, the next highest authorizations, for the Missouri Quality Jobs tax credit
and the Historic Preservation tax credit, were approximately $100 million each, with $133
million in redemptions for the Historic Preservation tax credit, and $30 million in
redemptions for the Missouri Quality jobs tax credit.

How do tax credits affect local vs. state tax revenue?
The majority of tax credits are aimed at reducing individual and corporate state income tax
(Office of Administration 2024). The most common local tax relief provided by statewide
statute is property tax relief, typically for seniors and disabled adults.

An important component of local taxation is the limit imposed by the Hancock Amendment
(MO Constitution Article X § 16, §22). Localities are prohibited from having windfall

revenues that exceed previous years’ budgets  adjusted for inflation.  This was  intended to
ensure reasonable  tax increases  by ensuring minimal budget increases  . In practice,
however, while the total income for entities like school districts cannot exceed previous
budgets, individuals may see  extreme  fluctuations  in their tax bills depending on home
valuations  . More information is available in the Science Notes Property Taxes and Home
Values, and Property Tax Assessment Limits.

Report on the State of Tax Credits in  Missouri

Missouri currently has 69 reported tax credits, 58 of which are active (Office of
Administration 2024). The other 11 have passed their sunset date or are otherwise
inoperable, although four still allow redemptions, and one has the authority to continue to
issue credits (Table 2). In FY24, Missouri authorized a total of $518,513,906 in tax credits,
issued $429,636,178 of those, and saw $906,921,654 redeemed. Of Missouri’s FY24 $15.2
billion budget, nearly $1 billion of potential revenue is expended on tax credits, or roughly
6% of the budget.

While there have been several spikes in the amount of tax credits authorized – whether
through the introduction of new credits or the raising of authorization limits through statute
– the amount of credits issued has remained relatively steady between $400 and $500
million (excluding 2023, Figure 10). However, the dollar amount of credits redeemed has
slowly risen to exceed issuances,  diverting after 2007. This may be due to the number of
entitlement credits introduced (see more in Entitled vs. Discretionary Tax Credits). Since
2007, at least one entitlement credit has been introduced per year, with 5 new entitlement
credits issued in 2023 (Figure 11).

Policy Research

What is the statute that allows the Department of Economic
Development to issue credits for greater amounts than were
appropriated?
The statute under which the tax credit was initially passed determines the parameters
under which it operates (see What are tax credits and how do they work?). There are two
types of tax credits: entitlement and discretionary, discussed in the earlier section titled
Entitled vs. Discretionary Tax Credits.

For example, some credits grant directors discretionary power for the dollar amount of
credits authorized or issued. The Missouri Development Finance Board (MDFB), housed
within the Department of Economic Development (DED), is authorized to increase the limit
for tax credits with the consent of multiple department directors, including the Directors of
the Department of Revenue, Department of Economic Development, and the
Commissioner of Administration (Office of Administration 2024, RSMo 100.286, Figure 3).
These amounts may be higher than  the legislature has accounted for in the budget.
What have other states done to manage the dollar amount and number of
tax credits?
States generally manage tax credits using sunset and authorization cap measures (NCSL
2024). Sunsets are discussed in detail in the ‘What are the effects of sunsets on tax
credits?’ section.  Authorization caps limit the amount of money that a tax credit can be
issued for a given year  , and are set in statute  (Office of Administration 2024  ). However,  tax
credits may be redeemed years after they are issued, even  after the sunset date has
passed  . These are known as ‘outstanding’  redemptions.  Redemptions can take place in
different years than issuances because of carry forward and carry back measures, which
allow entities to claim the credit on tax credits in future or past tax years.  The  number of
years a tax credit can be carried forward or back  is determined by statute, and each tax
credit operates under different provisions for these timelines.

In some cases  , a tax credit can be authorized for an amount larger than is issued, if no  t
enough entities apply for the tax credit.  Tax credits that must be applied for are
‘discretionary’ as opposed to ‘entitled’ which automatically apply during tax filing (  Office of
Administration 2024). More information about this is available in the Sections on
Authorization, Issuance, and Redemption  – Tax Credit Process and Entitled vs.
Discretionary Tax Credits.

How does this change as the economy  changes?
Tax credits, or tax expenditures, reduce taxpayer liability and the total state revenue. As
with other state budgetary expenditures and programs, states may choose to reexamine tax
credit legislation during times of economic change, particularly downturns.

The Great Recession
During the Great Recession (2007-2009) and its aftermath, states saw an increased need
for state services concurrent with a steep loss in state revenue (Johnson et al. 2010,
Federal Reserve History 2013). Balanced budgets required that states either increase
revenue generation through new mechanisms or cut spending. In the wake of the 2009
recession, nearly all states cut spending, and 33 opted to create new revenue streams in
2009 (Figure 16). These were achieved by eliminating tax exemptions, broadening tax
bases, and in some cases increasing rates  and fees (Langley 2014). By 2012, 40 states had
enacted tax or fee hikes (Gordon 2012). Raising new revenue as a response to a recession
has been shown to provide more short-term economic benefits than cuts alone, and does
not have an adverse effect for long-term economic recovery and performance (Johnson et
al. 2010). Typically, these tax increases come from personal income and sales taxes, with
some states opting to increase corporate taxes. Missouri did not raise revenue by any
mechanisms in response to the Great Recession.

Changes to tax laws predominantly focused on increasing tax rates for already existing
taxes, subjecting more items or purchases to existing taxes, or eliminating tax credits,
deductions, and exemptions (Johnson et al. 2010, Table 7). Some states added additional
income tax brackets to raise tax rates on the highest earners during this period, although
nearly all these provisions contained sunsets.  In contrast, some states, including Missouri,
cut taxes in this time period (Gordon 2012).

Because many of these tax changes were temporary, they had a limited effect on revenue
shortfalls (Langley 2014). State budget shortfalls increased in Fiscal Year 2012, and
subsequent state spending cuts most heavily impacted local government budgets. Local
governments also rely heavily on property taxes, which decreased as a result of home
devaluations. K-12 education depends on both state funding and local property taxes, and
thus experienced some of the highest budget reductions during this period.

The Coronavirus Pandemic
During the height of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic (2020-2021), states focused on
tax relief (Chen & Hathaway 2024). High tax revenues and federal aid created large fiscal
reserves, allowing states to provide both broad and targeted relief measures  (Figure 17).
The two largest relief categories were income tax relief and sales tax relief  , which make up
75% of all state tax revenues. In Missouri, income tax and sales tax account for  more than
90% of the state’s general revenue (GR)  (Figure 18). Individual income tax alone accounts
for 60-70% of the state’s GR, with sales taxes  making up slightly more than 20% of state
revenue (MO Senate Appropriations Committee 2022, MO Senate Appropriations
Committee 2021, MO Senate Appropriations Committee 2020, MO Senate Appropriations
Committee 2019, MO Senate Appropriations Committee 2018, MO Senate Appropriations
Committee 2017). Increasingly, more state revenue has come from other taxes, including
taxes on specific products or services, and there has been a slight increase (~1%) in
corporate income tax generated GR.

Research shows that increasing taxes on business activities that bring individuals in close
contact can encourage businesses to create alternative methods of service delivery that
protect workers and customers from communicable disease (Craig & Hines 2020). It also
shows that the reduced consumer choice available during the pandemic reduced the
welfare cost of raising taxes on higher-income taxpayers, and was an optimal time for
deficit closure.

States reduced taxes by lowering rates and creating or expanding tax credits, exemptions,
and deductions (Chen & Hathaway 2024, Table 8). Some states raised additional revenue

by increasing tax rates on high earners and capital gains, but no states removed tax credits
or deductions to increase revenue.

How does tax credit management affect the state budget?
Tax credits, or tax expenditures, reduce tax liability and state income. Tax credits can
provide relief or incentivize business or consumer behavior, but can also reduce the state’s
capacity to provide services. Without periodic review, sunsets, or other legislative action,
tax credits may increase in number and outlive the economic conditions under which they
were created (Gross et al. 2012, Gross et al. 2010). In this case, along with inevitable
addition of tax credits to address new state needs, the result will be an increasing
reduction in the state budget, and a vulnerability to future economic crises (Chen &
Hathaway 2024).
What are the effects of sunsets on tax credits?
Sunset provisions create temporary legislation that governs for a predetermined period of
time (Fagan 2013). Typically, legislation is permanent unless repealed and governs
indefinitely. Tax credits under sunset also apply temporarily, unless renewed.

Regulatory legislation under sunset has been shown to affect the compliance of entities
(i.e. individuals and businesses) after its expiry, even when that compliance isn’t enforced

44

[PDF page 46]
by any state actors (Fagan 2013). This means that temporary legislation can have impacts
on individual and organizational behavior  even after it has expired, especially if it is costly
to readjust to changing conditions. In this way, sunset provisions have been used to pass
permanent changes as temporary legislation. In addition, because sunset provisions can
be extended, they can be used to effectively create permanent legislation (Sutherland
2019).

Like other legislative sunsets, tax credit sunsets have been proposed as a means of
dislodging entrenched interest groups, giving legislators flexible tools for new needs and
problems as they arise, transforming stagnant governments, and ensuring restrained
lawmaking in the face of temporary trouble (Kysar 2006). When originally proposed at the
federal level, sunsets were an attempt to force periodic evaluations of government
programs, including tax credits (Penner & Korb 1976). However, it was identified at the time
that evaluating government programs is a complex task, and that no metric exists to
compare programs with vastly different outputs, goals, and structures. Additionally,
researchers identified that political interests and will could override evaluations showing
inefficient or ineffective programs.

In more recent years, sunset provisions have been attached to entire tax code acts at the
federal level such as the Economic Growth and Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2001, the
Jobs and Growth Tax Relief Reconciliation Act of 2003, and the most recent Tax Cuts and
Jobs Act of 2017 (HR 1836 – 107th Congress (2001-2002), HR 2 – 108th Congress (2003-
2004), HR 1 – 115th Congress (2017-2018)). These sunsets have been constructed in
response to fiscal controls in the budget process, rather than for the purpose of imparting
legislative flexibility or restrained lawmaking (  Kysar 2006). Attaching sunsets to tax credit
legislation allows for underestimation of revenue costs by constraining analysis to the
sunset period, even though the legislature may extend the credits  , and has been used to
avoid checks on legislative budgeting (Viswanathan 2007). Additionally, research has found
that after enactment, sunset provisions reduce the reliability of revenue estimates,
especially beyond the possible renewal date.

Tax credit sunsets, particularly at the local level,  can be effective if applied to short term
funding projects with specific goals (Shybalkina 2022  ). For example, tax credits for
transportation infrastructure, capital funding, bond financing, and public safety projects.  To
be most effective, research suggests that tax credits be applied to a specific short  -term
need, not as a stand  -in for long term funding  . Additional requirements for effectiveness
include clear guidelines and definitions, alignment of the tax credit with beneficiaries,
establishment of citizens review for accountability, and  transparency throughout the life of
the sunset.

45

[PDF page 47]
Utilizing sunset and reauthorization  measures to create semi-permanent legislation can
create boom and bust cycles within industries that ultimately lead to higher costs and
instability (Dewey 2011). This is especially true if projects take longer than the  sunset’s
timeline. For example, renewable energy projects eligible for the federal Production Tax
Credit often take 5-7 years, while the credit itself is only applicable for 1-3 years.
Additionally, sunset provisions can harm low resource beneficiaries of tax credits and
increase the ability of highly organized, well-funded groups to lobby for reauthorization of
tax credit legislation (Kysar 2006).

Sunset provisions typically allow for eligible entities to redeem the credit even after the
sunset date, which impacts budgets and annual revenue in subsequent years (MO State
Auditor 2017). However, some credits expire upon their sunset, which can compound the
boom-and-bust challenges for industries with longer term projects (Dewey 2011).

In MO, both sunsets and period reviews have been suggested as a way to manage tax
credits (Gross et al. 2012, Van Matre et al. 2012, Gross et al. 2010). In the 2010 Report of
the Missouri Tax Credit Review Commission, the Commission recommended that the
General Assembly impose sunset provisions on tax credit  programs and provided a sunset
schedule for consideration (Gross et al. 2010, Table 9). Tax credits scheduled for sunset
could be extended or authorized to continue by new legislation.  In a subsequent report, the
Commission reversed its recommendation for sunset provisions and instead
recommended periodic review (Gross et al. 2012). Rather than subject tax credits to the
annual appropriations process, another suggestion of the 2010 Commission,  the 2012
Commission recommended that the General  Assembly should instead periodically review
all tax credit programs using standardized evaluation criteria  . These should include the
return on investment (ROI) to the state, the economic impact, and cost effectiveness of
each credit program.

The reason given for this change was fear that sunsets would impede continuity of tax
credit availability by subjecting credits to legislative politics and gridlock  (Van Matre et al.
2012). In particular, the filibuster was cited as a threat to  reauthorization.

How do tax credits affect the MO budget over  time?
Legally, tax credits are treated as grants of state money, but constitutions have virtually no
legal grounds to challenge credits, even if they feel they are a misuse of funds (Maanzara et
al. v. State of Missouri et al. 2011). For more information on the legal framework for tax
credits, see the earlier section on Legal Framework for Missouri Tax Credits  .

Tax credits are sometimes referred to as “tax expenditures” because they are considered
the equivalent of spending by the state (GAO 2024, Phares 2003). Rather than collecting
revenue and returning it to beneficiaries, the tax credit provides that the revenue is simply
not collected. To this end, some researchers refer to tax credits as a subsidy. Ultimately, tax
credits result in a loss of tax revenue for the state.

Over time, a greater share of the Missouri state budget has come from federal funding
sources. For more information, see the Science Note History of MO Taxes. In short, from
1994 to 2024, GR funds raised by the state have decreased from 42% to 29% of the total
budget, with federal funds rising from 27% to 47% over the same period (MO House 2023,
MO House 2002, Figure 19).

In 2010 it was reported that MO spent roughly the equivalent of 8% of its GR budget on tax
credit redemptions (Gross et al. 2010). By comparison, in 1998, Missouri redeemed tax
credits constituted 1.7% of GR for that year (Figure 20). In 2024 this number is 6% of GR.
Higher tax expenditures are becoming a consistent part of the state budget, thereby
reducing the discretionary spending capabilities of the state.

Are there good metrics for determining the ROI of tax credits in  MO?
There are two major models used  by Missouri for examining the impact or value of a tax
credit: IMPLAN and REMI (MO Office of Administration 2024  ).

The Impact Analysis for Planning (IMPLAN) model was developed in 1976 by the United
States Forest Service (USFS) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to
estimate the economic effects of resource outputs on local communities (IMPLAN 2024).
IMPLAN was maintained by the USFS until 1985, at which point the responsibility of
developing data sets shifted to the University of Minnesota to accommodate increasing
demand. Eventually, non-USFS organizations began to use the data sets, at which point the
IMPLAN (originally Minnesota IMPLAN Group) was established under MIG, Inc. as an
independent corporation to develop and sell the IMPLAN database and software.

IMPLAN uses Input-Output (I-O) analysis (IMPLAN 2023). IO economic modeling assumes
that all industries, households, and government entities in the economy are connected
through buy-sell relationships (Figure 21). Thus, under this model, all economic activities
have ripple effects that impact the entire economy.  IMPLAN uses annual regional data to
map these relationships in an effort to estimate how  individual economic changes may

49

[PDF page 51]
impact an entire regional economy. A benefit of IMPLAN is that analysts can see all data
used in the models and are able to customize it with local data and on  -the-ground
knowledge.

The Regional Economic Models, Inc. (REMI) model was developed in 1980  to assist
government decision-makers in testing the impact of policies before  implementation (REMI
2024a). REMI employs multiple models, each with a specific focus (  REMI 2024b). These
include economic impact models for general, transportation, tax, energy and environment
policies, and a model to measure the socio  -economic impact of general policies.

REMI is the most complex and comprehensive economic modeling program, combining
traditional IO modeling w  ith relationship modeling between other economic variables such
as employment, prices, and income (  Neill 2013). REMI models are able to capture market
dynamics and consumer behaviors more comprehensively than traditional IO models.

In MO, departments have used these two models to estimate the cost  -benefit impact of
some tax credits (MO Office of Administration 2024  ). However, because tax credit
programs vary widely in their directive, purpose, and administration,  direct comparisons
are difficult (MO House Budget Office, personal communication).

For example, the MO Diaper Bank Tax Credit  is claimed by individual or corporate taxpayers
who donate to diaper banks in MO (  RSMo 135.621). This credit is intended to incentivize
donations to diaper banks, with the aim that diaper bank clients will access services
through the diaper bank, rather than using state assistance (MO Office of Administration
2024). The direct impacts of this credit (i.e. the number of donations to diaper banks and
the number of clients served) are more easily quantified than other tax credits.

By contrast, the State and Local Taxes (SALT) Parity Act allows small businesses (i.e. not
large, publicly traded  corporations) and/or partnerships (e.g. syndicates, groups, pools,
joint ventures, or unincorporated organizations)  to combine as one entity and pay taxes  on
the sum of their assets (IRS 2024c, RSMo 143.436, 26 U.S.C. 79 § 7701(a)(2)). Members of
this larger entity are then entitled to a credit against their state income tax.

SALT Parity Acts are intended to circumvent limits imposed by the 2017 Tax Cuts and Job
Act (TCJA) (S-Corp 2023). Prior to TCJA, most individuals and entities were able to deduct
the amount paid to state and local taxes from their federal tax burden. The TCJA limits the
amount that can be deducted to $10,000 (HR 1 – 115th Congress (2017-2018)). This means
for individuals and entities paying more than $10,000 in  state and local taxes, the taxes
owed above that limit will also apply at the federal level.  The SALT cap was intended to raise
revenue to offset the $7.4 trillion estimated loss in federal tax revenue (York et al. 2024).
SALT Parity Acts disproportionately benefit higher income individuals, particularly those in
high local tax areas, by reducing their federal income tax liability (Watson 2023). Because
this credit effectively returns income to individuals by reducing their tax liability, it is
difficult to quantify direct impacts beyond this liability reduction.

To this end, while impact modeling is possible for some credits, others do not lend
themselves easily to comparative analysis. Reducing credits to a cost-benefit analysis
score may minimize the impact of social or non-economic benefits, or otherwise create
uneven comparisons. Ultimately, the only thing all tax credits have in common is that they
reduce tax liability and thus tax revenue (Phares 2003).

How does the Hancock Amendment affect credits and generating excess
revenue?
Article X § 18 of the Missouri Constitution, commonly known as the Hancock Amendment,
limits the taxes which may be imposed by the MO General Assembly (MO Constitution Art.
X § 18). This limit requires that the ratio between the total state revenue and the personal
income of Missourians be the same as the one calculated for certain base years. Excess
state revenue beyond 1% of this limit must be refunded proportionally to Missouri state
income taxpayers (MO Constitution Art. X § 18). The Hancock Amendment also limits the
amount of new revenue the General Assembly may raise each year through taxes and fees
without a vote of the people.

Total state revenue is defined as the funds received in the state treasury and subject to
appropriation (Kelly v. Hanson 1997). This includes but is not limited to general revenue,
special revenue, licensing fees, and other miscellaneous fees (Kevin-Myers & Hembree
2012). In 1981, the Hancock ratio between personal income and the state budget was set
at 5.6395% and has not changed since (Kevin-Myers & Hembree 2012, MO State Auditor
2024a). In 2023, the MO budget cap was calculated at more than $19.5 billion and the state
revenue $15.1 billion ($4.4 billion below the threshold). The Hancock cap on new state
revenue was $132.8 million in 2023, however the state decreased revenue by $773.2
million in FY23.

Tax credits, on average, reduce total state revenue as defined for the Hancock Amendment
(Missouri Merchants v. State 2001, Kevin-Myers & Hembree 2012). The exception is tax
credits which exceed the amount of money owed in taxes, i.e. refundable tax credits (for an
example see What are tax credits and how do they work?).

Tax and fee revenues that are directly approved by voters after the adoption of the Hancock
Amendment are exempt from its provisions (  Goode v Bond 1983, MO Constitution Art. X §
18).

The Hancock Amendment applies to both state and local government funding  . Political
subdivisions and local governments are not to increase taxes and fees without voter
approval (MO Constitution Art X § 22, Blankenship v. Franklin County Collector 2021).
However, it also prevents the state from shifting funding responsibilities to the local level by
requiring that any new programs mandated to local governments by the state must be
funded by the state (MO Constitution Art X § 16, MO Constitution Art X § 21).

55

[PDF page 57]
Is MO Close to hitting the Hancock ceiling?
If the total state revenue exceeds the  limit set by the ratio to the personal income of
Missourians, the state must refund this amount proportionally to income taxpayers (  MO
Constitution Art. X § 18). MO has not exceeded the Hancock limit since 1999 (MO State
Auditor 2024a). In 2023, the MO budget was $4.4 billion below the Hancock budget limit,
and $906 million below the new revenue limit (by decreasing revenue by more than $773
million).

MO has only exceeded the Hancock limit five times, all in the 1990s (Figure 22). The
difference between the total revenue and the Hancock limit  since 2010 has averaged more
than $4 billion per year (Figure 23). In the past decade, MO has exceeded the cap on new
revenue once (Figure 24).

While Missouri has room to raise roughly $4 billion in revenue before risking the Hancock
limit, the limit on new revenue generation makes this difficult to achieve in a single fiscal
year.

Who is held accountable for tax credits?
Tax credit information is freely available online through multiple sources, including the
Office of Administration’s (OA’s) Tax Credit Analysis Forms and the Governor’s Missouri
Accountability Portal (MAP) (MO Office of Administration 2024, State of Missouri 2024). The
MAP allows individuals to parse tax credits by category, legislative district, and to look up
individual credit redemptions if they know the redeeming entity. Additionally, the OA
provides information about the individuals who administer specific tax credits, and their
contact information, on the Tax Credit Analysis Forms.

However, individual Missourians who feel a tax credit is a misuse of public funds cannot
challenge the credit in court without a “direct and particular connection to it,” (Maanzara,
et al. v. State of Missouri, et al. 2011, Van Matre et al. 2012). Because tax credits are not
classified as government expenditures, their effect on general taxpayers is considered
speculative. Thus, individuals challenging tax credits in court are required to provide
specific proof of harm.

The only recourse for individual Missourians to challenge tax credits is through their
elected representatives in the legislature. Legislators may take legislative action  to change
or cancel tax credits that are not already redeemed and have a duty to ensure that tax
credits are constitutional (Van Matre et al. 2012).

Research suggests that the Maanzara decision has led the legislature to use tax credits as
an alternative to direct expenditures (  Dabson et al. 2013). Tax credits are less expensive to
operate than standard expenditure programs, because they require significantly less
oversight and accountability. However, by using tax credits as an alternative to
expenditures, the legislature has ceded control of the associated budget scrutiny and
accountability measures.
